issues.item: Threat in Movements: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
issues.explanation: The threat items imply a trauma context dominated by interpersonal assault or ambush cues (others' sudden movements, ominous silence) rather than toxic chemical exposure. For a chemical exposure trauma, these are hard to reconcile unless there is additional unreported assault/combat context.

issues.item: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal about losing connection to community/culture is not well anchored to the rest of the profile. The other selected items center on intrusive memory, overwhelm, and coping incapacity, but there are no related triggers, memories, or strategies suggesting social/cultural disconnection as a core post-trauma theme.

issues.item: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: This item is the least coherent with the rest of the profile. For a 72-year-old married male Coast Guard patient with toxic chemical exposure, the dominant pattern elsewhere is threat, intrusive sensory memory, and low coping around reminders. 'Lost connection to my community and culture' is not impossible, but it is not well supported by the trauma type or by the other selected threat/memory/appraisal items, which center on danger, overwhelm, and inability to handle recall. It reads as a broader social-identity consequence that is disconnected from the active formulation, where Memory and Threat are tightly linked and Negative Appraisals are threat-focused. This makes that individual appraisal item clinically weakly matched to the rest of the self-report.

vignette:
Eugene, a 72-year-old African American man, had spent most of his adult life in the Coast Guard, the kind of work he had once taken pride in for its discipline and clear routines. The event that now shadows him happened years ago on a cutter during a chemical spill exercise gone wrong, when a toxic vapor escaped unexpectedly into a compartment and people shouted for masks while alarms cut through the metal corridors. Eugene remembers the moment with the sharpness of a photograph: the yellow warning signs, the slick floor, the faces of crewmen turning toward the hatch, and the choking sensation that made him feel he could not get enough air. Even now, when the memory comes back, it arrives like a film he cannot stop, each frame returning with the same force, and he has to break off mid-thought because the emotion floods him so quickly.

Since then, Eugene has come to believe that the world is a dangerous place and that he cannot deal with even the slightest upset. He says that if he thinks about that day for too long, he will not be able to handle it, and that small problems are enough to overwhelm him because he already knows how fast things can turn. Those beliefs make ordinary moments feel loaded with danger. When the house is unusually quiet, or when he notices silence where there should be a radio, footsteps, or his wife moving about the kitchen, he feels something bad is about to happen. He remains on guard even inside his own home, listening for changes in sound, watching the hallway, and bracing his body for what might come next. What frightened him most after the spill was not only the exposure itself but the conviction that his body and mind had already shown they could not cope, and that sense of low coping now keeps his vigilance high.

That vigilance, in turn, seems to pull the memory back at him. Eugene describes sitting alone in the living room when the house goes quiet and suddenly feeling the old scene rush in again, as if the smell, the alarms, and the panic have been stored just beneath the surface and are waiting for any lapse in noise. At those moments, the event replays in his mind with painful vividness: the compartment, the shouted orders, the helplessness of not knowing whether the air itself was harming him. The more these images return, the more certain he becomes that he is not equipped to tolerate them, and the more firmly he concludes that the world cannot be trusted. He does not speak of this in abstract terms; it shows in the way he becomes tense and watchful after even a brief reminder, interpreting the return of the memory as proof that danger is still close and that he must stay ready.

Over the years, Eugene has organized his days around avoiding that mental collapse. He tries not to think about the incident, steering away from conversations about his Coast Guard service and quickly changing the subject if the spill or chemicals are mentioned. Yet the effort to keep it away has not made him feel safer; instead, it has left him more alert for any sign of danger and more easily pulled back into the same flood of images. In his house, he checks doors more often, sits where he can see the hallway, and is unsettled when the television is off and the rooms are too still. His wife has noticed that he seems distant in those moments, as if a small pause in sound can put him back on the ship. He has begun turning on background noise just to get through the evening, but even then he stays watchful, as though silence itself might open the door to the old film.

What brought Eugene to seek help was that the pattern has become harder to hide, even from himself. He recently found that he could not finish a family dinner when the room fell quiet after an argument, because the silence made him feel danger in the walls and the memory surged so strongly he had to leave the table. He fears that if this keeps on, he will lose the steadiness he has always associated with being a husband and former service member, and he is most afraid that one day the images and the alarm in his body will become the only way he knows how to live. At the same time, he is hoping for some relief from the constant sense that disaster is about to begin.
